cards.term: When Eli Whitney invented the cotton gin
cards.def: Eli Whitney invented the cotton gin in 1793, and by 1840 the South produced more than 60 percent of the world's cotton and almost two-thirds of all U.S. exports.

cards.term: How much the cotton gin sped cleaning
cards.def: The gin let one laborer clean 50 pounds of short-fiber cotton a day, compared with 1 pound by hand.

cards.term: When the Second Bank and the Tariff of 1816 were enacted
cards.def: In 1816 Congress chartered the Second Bank of the United States for 20 years and passed a mildly protective tariff averaging a 20 percent duty.

cards.term: When the Clermont ran
cards.def: Robert Fulton's Clermont ran from New York City to Albany on the Hudson in 1807.

cards.term: Span of the Erie Canal's construction
cards.def: New York built the 364-mile Erie Canal from 1818 to 1825, from Albany on the Hudson to Buffalo on Lake Erie.

cards.term: How much the Erie Canal cut freight costs
cards.def: The cost per ton from Buffalo to New York City fell from more than 19 cents a mile to less than 3 cents a mile, and to less than 1 cent by 1860.

cards.term: Canal mileage by 1840
cards.def: By 1840 the United States had more than 3,300 miles of canals, built at a cost of about $125 million, almost half of it from state governments.

cards.term: How much land transport improved from 1825 to 1855
cards.def: From 1825 to 1855, the cost of land transport fell 95 percent and speed rose five-fold.

cards.term: How steamboats changed the western rivers
cards.def: Steamboats cut the New Orleans-to-Louisville trip from 90 days to 8 and upstream costs by 90 percent, and their number rose from 17 in 1817 to 727 in 1855.

cards.term: When rail mileage caught up with canals
cards.def: The United States had only 13 miles of track in 1830, but by 1840 rail and canal mileage were equal at 3,325 miles, and by 1850 there were 8,879 miles of track.

cards.term: When Morse patented the telegraph
cards.def: Samuel Morse patented the telegraph in 1837, and by 1860 there were more than 50,000 miles of telegraph lines; the first intercity message was sent in 1844.

cards.term: The U.S. postal system in 1840
cards.def: In 1840 the postal system carried about 41 million letters and 39 million newspapers, and in 1828 the United States already had almost twice as many post offices as Great Britain and more than five times as many as France.

cards.term: When key Marshall Court cases were decided
cards.def: Fletcher v. Peck was decided in 1810, McCulloch v. Maryland and Dartmouth College v. Woodward in 1819, and Gibbons v. Ogden in 1824.

cards.term: U.S. population growth to 1850
cards.def: Population doubled about every 22 years, from fewer than 4 million in 1790 to more than 23 million in 1850.

cards.term: How fast American cities grew, 1820-1860
cards.def: Cities of 5,000 or more rose from 12 in 1820 to nearly 150 in 1850, and the farmer-to-city ratio fell from 15-to-1 in 1800 to 5.5-to-1 in 1850, the fastest urbanization in U.S. history.

cards.term: When the Lowell mills were established, and mill-girl pay
cards.def: The Boston Associates established the Lowell mills in 1820, and mill girls earned $2.40 to $3.20 a week, compared with less than $1 a week for domestics and seamstresses.

cards.term: When the Lowell workforce shifted to Irish immigrants
cards.def: Irish workers were 8 percent of the Lowell workforce in 1845 and almost half by 1860, as wages declined and a permanent working class formed.

cards.term: When the National Trades' Union was founded
cards.def: The National Trades' Union was founded in 1834, then lost momentum in the Panic of 1837.

cards.term: How much cotton-cloth prices fell
cards.def: From 1815 to 1860 the price of cotton cloth fell from 18 cents a yard to 2 cents a yard.

cards.term: How concentrated wealth became
cards.def: The top 1 percent in major northeastern cities owned a quarter of the wealth in 1825 and half by 1850, and by 1860 5 percent of families owned more than half the nation's wealth.

cards.term: When the Panic of 1819 struck, and the cotton-price collapse
cards.def: The Panic of 1819 followed a boom in which Liverpool cotton reached 32.5 cents a pound in 1818, then prices collapsed, land values fell 50 to 75 percent almost overnight, and New Orleans cotton had already been driven down to 14 cents when English mills imported Indian cotton in 1816-1817.

cards.term: The later boom-and-bust cycle after 1819
cards.def: A second cycle brought the Panic of 1837 and a severe depression from 1839 to 1843, and a third ended in the depression that began in 1857.
